Name: answer_commitment_probe
Title: When Does the Model Already Know? Probing Answer Commitment to Enable Mechanistic Early-Exit in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: During a long chain-of-thought (CoT), a reasoning model internally 'commits' to its final answer many tokens before it verbalizes it. This commitment is linearly decodable from the residual stream. If we can detect the commitment point online with a cheap probe, we can terminate reasoning early and emit the answer, cutting generation cost substantially without retraining and without hurting accuracy.
Related Work: Efficient-reasoning methods (adaptive CoT length via RL, difficulty-conditioned routing, self-awareness signals) reduce token usage but require training or explicit difficulty labels. Confidence-based early-exit (e.g., self-consistency truncation, entropy thresholds) uses output-distribution signals, not internal state. Interpretability work shows models encode answers in intermediate layers (logit lens, tuned lens) and that CoT can be unfaithful, but has not built an online early-exit controller around a measurable 'answer commitment' event. Our proposal is distinct: we define and empirically characterize a mechanistic answer-commitment point via linear probes on the residual stream during ongoing generation, then convert it into a training-free early-exit controller and study when internal commitment diverges from verbalized reasoning (a faithfulness diagnostic).
Abstract: Long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning generates many tokens, but the model may internally decide on its answer well before it finishes reasoning. We hypothesize an 'answer commitment' point: a token position after which the model's residual-stream representation stably encodes the eventual final answer, so that further generation is largely redundant. We test this by training lightweight linear probes on hidden states at each generation step to predict the model's own final answer, tracking when the probe's prediction becomes correct and stable. We characterize the commitment point across math (GSM8K, MATH) and multiple-choice logic (ProntoQA, ARC) benchmarks and multiple open-weight reasoning models, measuring how far it precedes verbalization and how it scales with problem difficulty. We then build a training-free online early-exit controller: at each step, a fast probe estimates whether the committed answer has stabilized; once a stability criterion is met, we skip remaining reasoning and force answer emission. We evaluate accuracy versus tokens-generated Pareto curves against full CoT, fixed truncation, and entropy/confidence-based early exit. Beyond efficiency, comparing the internal commitment point to the verbalized reasoning yields a faithfulness diagnostic: cases where the model commits early but continues elaborating reveal post-hoc rationalization. We expect 25-45% token reduction at near-equal accuracy, plus a mechanistic account of when reasoning becomes computationally inert.
Experiments: 1. Commitment characterization: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, and Llama-3.1-8B, generate full CoT on GSM8K, MATH, ProntoQA, ARC. For each step, extract residual-stream hidden states across a few layers and train per-step linear probes to predict the model's own final answer (for MCQ: label id; for open math: bucketed/token-matched answer). Measure probe accuracy as a function of relative position; define commitment point as the earliest step after which probe prediction matches final answer and remains stable. 2. Scaling: Plot commitment position (fraction of CoT) vs. problem difficulty and CoT length; test whether commitment happens earlier for easy items. 3. Online controller: Use a single lightweight probe (or logit-lens readout) computed each K tokens; declare commitment when the predicted answer is unchanged for W consecutive checks with margin above threshold; then force '\nThe answer is' continuation. 4. Evaluation: accuracy vs. mean tokens generated (Pareto), wall-clock latency, against baselines: full CoT, fixed-length truncation, output-entropy early exit, self-consistency truncation. 5. Faithfulness diagnostic: quantify gap between internal commitment and verbalization; on cases with large gaps, test whether the verbalized reasoning ever changes the committed answer (rare = post-hoc). 6. Ablations: probe layer choice, stability window W and margin, cross-dataset and cross-model probe transfer, comparison to logit-lens (no trained probe) for a fully unsupervised variant.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. For hard problems, commitment may coincide with the end of reasoning, limiting savings; the Pareto analysis quantifies this. 2. Early exit may occur before the answer is actually correct if the probe reads a premature/incorrect commitment; the stability window mitigates but adds latency. 3. Open-ended answers are harder to probe than MCQ; we restrict open math to extractable numeric answers. 4. Probes may not transfer across models/datasets, requiring per-setting calibration; we test transfer explicitly. 5. Logit-lens readout may be noisy in some layers; the trained-probe variant is the fallback.
